name: AIIR Finance
tagline: A personal finance dashboard that pulls accounts together and puts an AI layer over spending, net worth and cash flow.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The visible half of a personal finance app is a solved problem: a table of transactions, a category mapper, some charts, and an LLM prompt that narrates your spending back to you. An agent will produce that in a session and it will feel surprisingly close. The part that does not survive is data intake: live bank and brokerage connections mean an aggregator contract, per-institution breakage, and someone whose job is fixing it on a Tuesday. Without that you are on CSV exports and manual updates, which is fine for a few weeks and then quietly rots. Also no phone app, so the daily habit loop is weaker than the hosted thing.
coreLoopDIY: Imports transaction and holdings CSVs into a local database, categorizes them with rules plus an LLM fallback, and renders net worth, cash flow and spending views with a chat box that queries your own numbers.
requirements: CSV or OFX exports from each bank, brokerage and card you care about
An LLM API key if you want the narration and auto-categorization
Somewhere to run it, laptop is fine, plus an actual backup plan for the database
Willingness to re-import manually, or pay for an aggregator like Plaid or SimpleFIN
whatYouLose: Automatic bank and brokerage sync, and the ongoing repair work when a connection breaks
A mobile app, so no glance-at-it-in-the-checkout-line habit
Categorization tuned on a lot of other people's messy merchant strings
Market data, FX rates and instrument metadata arriving without you thinking about it
Any story about encryption, recovery or support when your only copy of ten years of finances is on one machine
moatNotes: Nothing about the UI is defensible. The aggregator plumbing, the institution coverage list and the handling of financial data are the actual product.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because personal finance tools only work if they are effortless. The moment you have to remember to export a CSV, the data goes stale, the charts start lying, and you stop opening the app. Paying a few dollars a month buys the connections staying alive, the phone app that makes checking a reflex, and the mild comfort that someone else is responsible for the encryption. A local build is a better teaching tool and a worse habit.
notes: Build it if you want to actually understand your money; keep it if you turn out to be the kind of person who imports CSVs on a schedule.
prompt:
Build a local-first personal finance dashboard. Empty folder, no scaffolding questions, just make these choices and go.

Stack: Next.js with the App Router and TypeScript, Tailwind for styling, SQLite via better-sqlite3 with Drizzle ORM, Recharts for charts. Everything runs on localhost with `npm run dev`. No auth, no accounts, no hosted backend, no telemetry, no analytics.

Data model: accounts (name, type in cash/credit/investment/loan, currency, optional manual balance), transactions (date, account, description, raw_merchant, amount signed, category, subcategory, notes, hash for dedupe), holdings (account, ticker, quantity, cost_basis, manual_price), balance_snapshots (account, date, value), rules (match pattern, target category).

Intake: a CSV import screen where the user uploads a file, maps columns to fields once per institution, and saves that mapping as a named preset reused on future imports. Dedupe by content hash so re-importing an overlapping export does not double count. Also allow manual entry for accounts with no export.

Categorization: run rules first, exact and regex match on description. Anything unmatched goes into an Uncategorized queue. Add an optional LLM pass that batches uncategorized descriptions and suggests categories from a fixed taxonomy defined in one config file. Read OPENAI_API_KEY from .env and skip the pass gracefully if it is missing. When the user accepts a suggestion, offer to write it back as a rule.

Views: net worth over time from balance snapshots plus holdings valuation; monthly cash flow with income, spend and savings rate; spend by category with a month-over-month comparison; a searchable transaction table with inline category editing.

Chat: one text box that answers questions about the user's numbers by translating the question into a parameterized read-only SQL query against the local database, showing the query and the result table. Never let it write.

Also include: a seed script with fake data so the app is not empty on first run, `npm run export` that dumps every table to CSV, and `npm run backup` that copies the SQLite file to a timestamped path.

Explicitly out of scope: bank aggregation or Plaid, live market data, multi-user support, budgeting envelopes, mobile apps, deployment config.

Write a README that states plainly that this depends on the user manually exporting CSVs, and lists exactly what breaks if they stop.
